flashcards.q: What's the difference between a one-way door and two-way door decision, and who coined the terms in this context?
flashcards.a: Two-way door: cheap to reverse, decide fast at the lowest competent level. One-way door: expensive/impossible to reverse, decide slowly with more input. Popularized by Jeff Bezos's 2015 shareholder letter.

flashcards.q: Name the three checks for whether a decision is actually reversible, beyond API compatibility.
flashcards.a: Data/state lock-in (schemas, fine-tuned artifacts, eval harnesses), organizational lock-in (retraining, new pipelines/on-call shape), and blast radius (how many systems/teams depend on it being stable).

flashcards.q: What is the weighted scorecard formula and where should criteria come from?
flashcards.a: weighted_total = sum(weight * score) per candidate. Criteria must be derived from THIS decision's actual constraints (query pattern, team depth, scale, consistency need) — not a generic reusable checklist every option scores 'fine' on.

flashcards.q: What's the tell that a scorecard's weights were reverse-engineered to justify a pre-made decision?
flashcards.a: The chosen option wins on every single criterion. A real tradeoff produces a mixed picture where the winner loses on 1-2 criteria but wins on the ones weighted most important.

flashcards.q: What single question decides build vs. buy?
flashcards.a: Does this capability touch revenue, retention, margin, or a defensible moat (differentiation)? If yes, lean build; if it's undifferentiated plumbing everyone needs the same version of, lean buy.

flashcards.q: Why is 'build or buy' considered the wrong framing for an entire AI system in 2026?
flashcards.a: Most real systems are a blend across layers (infrastructure, model, orchestration, UX) — the actual question is which layers to own vs. delegate, not a single binary verdict for 'the AI system.'

flashcards.q: Why is an LLM/model vendor swap often more of a one-way door than the API surface suggests?
flashcards.a: Fine-tuning data, prompt engineering tuned to one provider's quirks, and evaluation harnesses built around one provider's output distribution don't transfer cleanly, even though the REST API interface looks interchangeable.

flashcards.q: Who introduced Architecture Decision Records and when, and what problem were they solving?
flashcards.a: Michael Nygard, 2011 blog post — solving 'we don't remember why we did this,' where decisions got re-litigated by people who weren't in the original room because reasoning lived only in someone's head.

flashcards.q: What section of an ADR do most teams skip, and why shouldn't they?
flashcards.a: Alternatives considered (with why each was rejected) — skipping it means the ADR only records the winner, not the reasoning that would let someone evaluate whether the tradeoff still holds later.

flashcards.q: When should a team NOT write an ADR for a technology decision?
flashcards.a: When it's low blast radius and reversible within a single team's effort (a routine dependency bump, an internal linter choice) — writing an ADR for everything drowns the signal of the ones that actually matter.

flashcards.q: What are the three steps to defending a technology choice under adversarial pushback?
flashcards.a: 1) Restate the constraint that drove the decision, not the decision itself. 2) Name concretely what would change your mind. 3) Concede the real tradeoff explicitly rather than defending every dimension as flawless.

flashcards.q: What ADR section prevents the same build-vs-buy debate from being re-litigated from scratch every 6 months?
flashcards.a: The 'what would change this decision' section — stating the concrete trigger/threshold for revisiting, so re-litigation only happens when that trigger actually fires.
